Pictures
pik'churz
n. pl. (images or carved representations; commanded to be destroyed in Canaan, and used in Proverbs for the setting of a well-spoken word)
Latin pictura, a painting, from pingere, to paint. The Hebrew varies: maskith in Numbers 33:52 is a figured stone or carved image; in Proverbs 25:11 the same root gives a setting or filigree of silver.

Biblical Definition

The first use is a command of destruction: “Then ye shall drive out all the inhabitants of the land from before you, and destroy all their pictures, and destroy all their molten images, and quite pluck down all their high places” (Numbers 33:52). Three objects, three verbs of demolition, and the whole apparatus of Canaanite worship is to go. Isaiah lists them among the objects of the day of the LORD: “And upon all the ships of Tarshish, and upon all pleasant pictures” (Isaiah 2:16) — commerce and art alike brought low when human loftiness is judged. But the word is not condemned in itself, and Proverbs proves it with one of the loveliest images in the book: “A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver” (Proverbs 25:11). The picture there is a setting, a worked frame of silver holding golden fruit, and the whole point is the beauty of the arrangement. The next verse continues it: “As an earring of gold, and an ornament of fine gold, so is a wise reprover upon an obedient ear” (Proverbs 25:12). Craftsmanship and beauty are not the problem. Worship is.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a picture as a painting exhibiting the resemblance of anything, and also any resemblance or representation.

expand to see more

PICTURE, n. A painting exhibiting the resemblance of any thing; a likeness drawn in colors.

2. The works of painters; painting.

3. Any resemblance or representation, either to the eye or to the understanding.

IMAGE, n. A representation or similitude of any person or thing, formed of a material substance.

2. An idol; the representation of any person or thing, that is an object of worship.

Key Scripture

Numbers 33:52 — "Then ye shall drive out all the inhabitants of the land from before you, and destroy all their pictures, and destroy all their molten images, and quite pluck down all their high places:"

Proverbs 25:11 — "A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in pictures of silver."

Isaiah 2:16 — "And upon all the ships of Tarshish, and upon all pleasant pictures."

Proverbs 25:12 — "As an earring of gold, and an ornament of fine gold, so is a wise reprover upon an obedient ear."

Modern Corruption

The second commandment is read either as a ban on art altogether or as a dead letter, and Scripture holds a narrower and more useful line.

expand to see more

Numbers 33:52 orders the destruction of images, and Proverbs 25:11 praises a worked setting of silver as a figure for good speech; the same Scriptures that command the smashing gave the pattern of the tabernacle in exhaustive artistic detail, with cherubim, pomegranates, blue and purple and scarlet, and named Bezaleel as filled with the Spirit of God in workmanship. The prohibition is not of representation but of representation for worship, and specifically of any image of God. The iconoclasm that treats all art as suspect has overshot the commandment; the Reformed tradition, which produced the Dutch masters and Bach, never held it.

The opposite corruption is the defence of images of Christ. The usual argument is that the incarnation makes it lawful to depict Him, since He took a real human nature. The Reformed churches have answered that the natures may not be divided: what is portrayed is the Person, and the Person is God, whom no man hath seen at any time. The Larger Catechism names images of God, of any of the three Persons, as forbidden by the second commandment. Whatever a believer concludes about art on a wall, the commandment's own scope is worship, and the pictures of Numbers 33 were destroyed for that reason and no other.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew maskith, a figured stone or carved image — Numbers 33:52, Leviticus 26:1; the same root for a setting or filigree — Proverbs 25:11; sekiyyah, imagery — Isaiah 2:16.

expand to see more

Hebrew maskith — a figure, an imagination, a carved stone; Numbers 33:52, Leviticus 26:1, and Proverbs 25:11 of a silver setting.

Hebrew massekah — a molten image; Numbers 33:52, the second of the three objects to be destroyed.

Hebrew bamah — a high place; Numbers 33:52, to be quite plucked down.

Hebrew sekiyyah — imagery, something looked at; Isaiah 2:16, the pleasant pictures brought low.

Exodus 31:3 shows the other side: Bezaleel filled with the Spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in all manner of workmanship.

Usage

"“Destroy all their pictures… and quite pluck down all their high places” — the object is worship."

"“Apples of gold in pictures of silver” — a worked setting, praised for its beauty."

"The same law that forbade the images gave the pattern for the tabernacle."
